newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British manufacturing picked up in Jan - survey.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British manufacturing picked up in Jan - survey.

text.p: The pace of growth in British manufacturing industry accelerated in January for the first time since October, according to a leading business survey published on Monday.

The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said its purchasing managers' index (PMI) rose to a seasonally adjusted 54.0 in January from 52.8 in December, signalling growth in manufacturing for the eighth month in a row.
"The improvement in the PMI was driven by an increase in the rate of growth of new orders," the institute said.

"Rising domestic demand (especially for consumer goods) provided the main impetus behind the boost to order books. Export demand, although subdued compared with the summer, continued to show modest growth."
The PMI is seen as a reliable barometer of activity in manufacturing. The snapshot it provides of the economy is often confirmed by subsequent official statistics.

The January survey followed a series of official data and business surveys which suggested the pace of economic growth in Britain might be slackening. Manufacturing output fell in November and retail sales fell in December.
The survey also brought good news on inflation.
It showed the pound's appreciation against other major currencies had led to a sharp fall in import prices, resulting in the sharpest drop in purchase prices since last August.

Economists said the survey was unlikely to persuade Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke that official interest rates should be raised this month to prevent inflation getting out of control.
Clarke holds his monthly monetary meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Wednesday.
The central bank chief has said he may press for rates to be increased to 6.50 percent from the present 6.0 percent at the meeting.
He is particularly concerned about strong money supply growth, which is widely seen as a pointer to future inflationary pressures.

The Bank said on Monday that M0, a narrow measure of money supply, accelerated to an annual rate of 7.4 percent in January from 7.0 percent in December. This is well outside the government monitoring range of zero to four percent.

But Clarke, who is anxious to avoid raising rates before the looming election, said in a television interview on Monday that recent data had justified his decision to reject the Bank's advice and leave interest rates unchanged in December.

"Since that meeting...all the information we have had about what is happening out there in the real economy points my way and really rather justifies my decison not to raise rates," he told BBC Television.
Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets, said the January survey was a little stronger than expected and should help to ease fears that manufacturing could be heading back towards recession.

"But with the recovery in industry still fragile and cost pressures still very subdued, the report is most unlikely to prompt Mr Clarke to raise interest rates at Wednesday's monetary meeting," he said.
